blocks.heading: Gross Domestic Product
blocks.text:
Gross Domestic Product is the value of final goods and services produced within an economy over a stated period. The location of production is central to domestic. The final-output condition avoids counting intermediate purchases repeatedly, and the period distinguishes the flow of new production from wealth accumulated over time. Goods and services both count; national production is not limited to physical factory items or government activity.

A privately owned repair business providing services within the economy contributes to domestic production even if some income later goes abroad. That later flow concerns the national adjustment rather than whether the service occurred domestically. A sale of an existing financial asset is not new production merely because it has a price. Similarly, a resale of an already produced item should not be treated as a second creation of the item’s whole value; a current service involved in the transaction is a separate question. Use the production and period described in the case. GDP is also not the government budget: public revenue and expenditure measure different flows. The term gross should be kept attached to the defined aggregate rather than silently equated with any net or differently valued national-income total. State the measurement basis before comparing figures.

blocks.heading: Gross National Product
blocks.text:
Gross National Product (GNP) is the total value of final goods and services produced by a country’s residents and their firms, at home or abroad, in a year. GNP = GDP + income received from abroad − income paid abroad. The relevant net figure is income received from abroad minus corresponding payments abroad. It is not the goods-trade balance, and it is not calculated simply by adding exports to GDP. Domestic production and the destination or source of factor income are different boundaries, so the adjustment can be positive or negative.

Suppose an exercise gives GDP N$800 million, income received abroad N$50 million and paid abroad N$35 million. Net primary income is N$15 million and GNP N$815 million on that stated basis. Reverse those income flows and GNP would be N$785 million instead. The sign follows the data rather than a rule that national product must exceed domestic product. A claim about one business being foreign-owned is insufficient to calculate the whole adjustment without amounts and the relevant accounting scope. These examples support the distinction without presenting nationality of a brand as an accounting definition. National accounts use economic residence and specified income flows, so avoid replacing that framework with a simple citizenship count. The purpose at this level is to identify the boundary and apply the supplied net-income adjustment consistently, keeping all figures in the same units and period. A negative net-income adjustment is written as subtraction from domestic product, not converted into a positive amount because it is called income. Keep receipts and payments in their stated directions. Check that GDP and the flows use matching units, since millions cannot be added directly to an unconverted number of individual dollars.

blocks.heading: National Income and factor rewards
blocks.text:
National Income is income generated by the factors of production of an economy over a stated period. The term needs its measurement basis when totals are compared. Labour, land, capital and enterprise contribute to production and receive relevant rewards under the applicable accounting arrangement. A measure of generated factor income differs from adding all cash received by households, because some receipts are transfers rather than new production income.

A household receiving a benefit does not create new output merely by receiving the payment. The transfer can support its spending, but including it again as factor income would confuse redistribution with production generation. A loan receipt likewise creates a financial obligation rather than directly measuring a factor reward. Wages paid for current production are a different kind of flow. These distinctions prevent a broad phrase money coming in from replacing an economic definition. Income methods also need to avoid double counting components and use consistent gross/net and valuation conventions. At this level, follow the basis supplied in the exercise instead of asserting that differently defined aggregates are exactly equal without adjustment. This links to GDP and GNP: the terms organise related but distinct questions about location, income flows and valuation. The data and definition together determine which total can be calculated, while a welfare conclusion still requires distribution and other evidence. A comparison should label its aggregate before drawing a conclusion. Two figures called income may refer to different boundaries or price bases, so their numerical difference alone can be misleading.

Gross figures include the value of machinery and buildings worn out during the year (depreciation, or capital consumption). Net National Product = GNP − depreciation, and this net figure at factor cost is conventionally called National Income; market-price figures require the appropriate tax and subsidy adjustment.
